sources.title: National Register of Historic Places listings in Davidson County, Tennessee
Wikipedia GeoSearch, 2 km around downtown Nashville (36.1627, -86.7816)

stops.name: Fort Nashborough
stops.description: A log stockade standing where James Robertson's party crossed the frozen Cumberland in 1780 and founded the city.

stops.name: Davidson County Courthouse and Nashville City Hall
stops.description: An eight-story Art Deco slab of Indiana limestone from 1937, still the mayor's office and the first air-conditioned building in the county.

stops.name: Printer's Alley
stops.description: A narrow cut between Union and Church that held thirteen publishers by 1915, then traded them for the nightclubs where Hendrix and Hank Williams played.

stops.name: Nashville Arcade
stops.description: A glass-roofed 1902 shopping arcade modelled on an Italian one, running clean through the block with matching Palladian faces at each end.

stops.name: Downtown Presbyterian Church
stops.description: William Strickland's 1849 church in full Egyptian Revival dress, lotus columns and a winged sun disk, pressed into service as a Union hospital in the Civil War.

stops.name: Ryman Auditorium
stops.description: Built as a gospel tabernacle in 1892 and known as the Mother Church of Country Music after housing the Grand Ole Opry from 1943 to 1974.

stops.name: Hermitage Hotel
stops.description: The Beaux-Arts hotel where both sides of the suffrage fight camped out in 1920 while Tennessee cast the vote that ratified the 19th Amendment.

stops.name: War Memorial Building
stops.description: A 1925 memorial carrying the names of 3,400 Tennesseans killed in the First World War, and the hall where Minnie Pearl joined the Opry.

stops.name: Tennessee State Capitol
stops.address: 600 Dr Martin Luther King Jr Blvd
stops.description: Strickland's Greek Revival statehouse of 1845 to 1859, holding the tombs of its own architect and of President James K. Polk.

stops.name: Hume-Fogg High School
stops.description: A 1912 Gothic Revival school standing on the site of Hume School, the first public school Nashville ever opened.

stops.name: Customs House
stops.description: Gothic Revival limestone raised between 1876 and 1882, an unusually ornate thing to build for a post office and a customs service.

stops.name: Frist Art Museum
stops.description: Nashville's Art Deco main post office of 1934, reopened in 2001 as a gallery that keeps no permanent collection of its own.

stops.name: Union Station
stops.description: A Romanesque Revival railroad terminal opened in 1900, whose tower once carried a bronze Mercury until a 1952 tornado took it down.

stops.name: Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum
stops.description: A building that reads as a bass clef from above, with windows set like piano keys and a roofline lifted from a 1959 Cadillac fin.

stops.name: John Seigenthaler Pedestrian Bridge
stops.description: A 1909 river crossing, the first in North America built on concrete arched trusses, handed over to walkers in 1998 and renamed for the civil rights journalist in 2014.

note: Nashville has never come up in this file before, so it wins outright on the longest-without-a-run rule. Worth knowing: the clone this run started from was SHALLOW, only 69 commits deep back to 2026-08-18, which hid every run before Jacksonville and would have made Atlanta look untouched. Ran git fetch --unshallow to recover the real history before picking. All 15 stops sit in a walkable downtown cluster, roughly Public Square down to Union Station, about a mile end to end. Two stops carry no address and no ZIP because they genuinely have no street number: Printer's Alley is an alley between 3rd and 4th Ave N, and the Seigenthaler bridge is a river span. Both have verified coordinates. Two ZIPs printed on Wikipedia were wrong and were corrected against independent sources: the Downtown Presbyterian Church infobox says 37201 and the church itself is in 37219, and the Customs House infobox says 37202, which is a PO box range, where the street ZIP for 701 Broadway is 37203. The Tennessee State Capitol address is the current street name, Dr Martin Luther King Jr Blvd, formerly Charlotte Ave. The Arcade's address is its 4th Avenue entrance per Nashville Downtown Partnership; the building runs through the block to 5th. Hume-Fogg is the one stop whose own article gave no address, so the address came from the school listing and the coordinates from the article's geotag. Dropped: Christ Church Cathedral at 900 Broadway, verified and walkable, cut only to stay inside the 15-stop ceiling; Musica and Marathon Motor Works, real and geotagged but well outside the downtown core; the Nathan Bedford Forrest Bust and the Carmack statue, both removed from their sites; Sulphur Dell and Sullivan Tower, both gone. The Wikipedia API rate-limited this session's shared proxy IP partway through, so verification moved to fetching the individual articles, which is the better check anyway.
